opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the constant-hazard-rate idea is basically: imagine that for every minute of human-equivalent work in a task, there's some fixed probability that the agent makes an unrecoverable mistake. If that's true, success probability decays exponentially with task length, and you get this nice clean picture where a single number, the hazard rate, or equivalently a characteristic time horizon, summarizes the model's capability.

I think it's a useful first-order model, and it captures something real. Longer tasks do have more steps where things can go wrong, and agents today often fail by going off the rails at some point and never recovering. So the qualitative shape, success dropping off as tasks get longer, is clearly there in the data.

But I'd be cautious about taking it too literally. A few things make me skeptical that it's the right functional form. One is that in our data, when we fit success against log task length, a logistic curve tends to fit reasonably well, and that's not quite what a pure exponential decay predicts. The tails behave differently. Models sometimes succeed on surprisingly long tasks and fail on surprisingly short ones, and a constant hazard rate doesn't really accommodate that heterogeneity.

Another is that the hazard isn't plausibly constant. Some parts of a task are much harder than others. There's often a crux, a key insight or a tricky debugging step, and most of the risk is concentrated there rather than spread evenly over time. Agents can also recover from mistakes sometimes, especially as they get better at checking their own work, which breaks the "one error and you're done" assumption.

And then there's the question of what "how long it takes humans" is even measuring. Human time is a proxy for difficulty, but it's a noisy one. Some tasks take humans a long time because they're tedious, not because they're hard, and AIs might find those comparatively easy. Others are short for humans but rely on tacit knowledge or context AIs lack.

So my overall take is: it's a nice simple model that gives you intuition and a reasonable headline metric, but I wouldn't lean on it for precise extrapolation. I'm more interested in empirically checking how the curve actually behaves, and in understanding what kinds of tasks deviate from the trend, because I think that's where a lot of the interesting information is.

r001.rationale: The response says a fixed probability of unrecoverable error per minute of human-equivalent work means success probability decays exponentially as task length increases.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we thought about a lot when we were putting together the time horizon paper at METR. The basic idea of the constant-hazard-rate model is that an AI agent has some fixed probability of failing per unit of human time on a task. So if a task takes a human an hour, and the model has, say, a one percent chance of making a fatal error per minute, then the chance of success falls off exponentially with task length. And the nice thing is that gives you a very clean, one-parameter curve: you fit the hazard rate, and that's basically your "time horizon."

I think it's a useful first approximation, and empirically it fits the data surprisingly well. When we plotted success rate against human completion time on the log scale, you do get something that looks like a logistic or sigmoid, which is roughly what the constant-hazard model predicts. So as a descriptive summary of where a model is right now, I think it's pretty reasonable, and it gave us a way to compare models over time that's a lot more meaningful than just saying "it got 60 percent on this benchmark."

But I'd be pretty cautious about taking it too literally as a mechanistic model of how AI systems actually fail. A few reasons. One is that the hazard almost certainly isn't constant in reality. Longer tasks aren't just more of the same minutes; they tend to have more interdependent steps, more state you have to keep track of, more opportunities for an early mistake to compound. So you'd expect the hazard rate to go up as the task gets longer, not stay flat. On the other hand, some long tasks are long for humans because they're tedious rather than hard, and models can sometimes blow through those, which pushes the other way. The constant-rate model kind of averages over all of that and hides it.

The second thing is that "how long it takes a human" is a pretty noisy proxy for difficulty. It depends a lot on which humans, how much context they have, how we measured it. In our data the human time estimates had quite a bit of variance, and that variance ends up getting baked into the fitted curve. So I think the horizon number should be read with wide error bars, and the trend over time, the doubling rate, is more robust than any individual point.

And third, the model says nothing about failure modes that aren't really about length at all. A model might fail on a five-minute task because it doesn't have some tool, or it misreads the instructions, or the environment is weird in a way that's orthogonal to how long a human would take. Those get lumped in as "hazard," but they're not really the thing the model is trying to capture.

So my overall take is: it's a good measuring stick, and I'd use it to track progress and make rough extrapolations. I would not use it to predict, for a specific task, whether a model will succeed, and I'd be especially careful extrapolating out to multi-week or multi-month tasks where we have basically no data and where I'd expect the structure of the problem to be qualitatively different. The honest answer is that it's a fit to the data we have, and the data we have is mostly software tasks under a few hours.

r001.rationale: The candidate says a fixed probability of failure per unit of human time means the chance of success “falls off exponentially with task length.”

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a useful baseline, but I’d be cautious about treating it as the underlying explanation. The idea is that the model has some fixed probability of failing per unit of task length, so its probability of successfully completing the whole task falls exponentially with length. That makes sense if a task consists of lots of steps, each of which presents a similar, independent opportunity for an unrecoverable mistake.

But human completion time isn’t necessarily a good measure of how many opportunities an AI system has to fail. A task might take a human a long time because it’s repetitive, while being quite easy for a model. Another might take an expert a minute but require an insight the model just doesn’t have. And failures needn’t be independent: an early mistake can make later mistakes more likely, or the system might notice an error and recover.

So I’d distinguish whether the model fits the observed data from whether it gives us reliable extrapolations. Even if it fits well over the task lengths we’ve measured, I’d want to check that on longer tasks and across different kinds of tasks before putting much weight on its predictions.

r001.rationale: The response says a fixed per-unit failure probability makes success probability fall exponentially with task length; in context, task length refers to human task duration.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a useful model to start with, but I’d be cautious about treating it as a general law. A constant hazard rate means that, conditional on having made it this far, the model has the same probability of failing in the next bit of the task. So the probability of completing the whole task falls exponentially with its length.

There’s a plausible intuition behind that: longer tasks give you more opportunities to make a mistake. But human completion time isn’t necessarily proportional to the number of opportunities an AI system has to fail. A task could take a human a long time because it involves a lot of repetitive work that’s very easy for the model, while a short task could contain one step the model simply can’t do.

And failures aren’t necessarily independent. An early mistake can make later mistakes more likely, or the system might notice a mistake and recover. You also have differences in difficulty across tasks. Even if a constant hazard model were reasonable within some particular kind of task, averaging across different kinds wouldn’t necessarily give you a constant hazard.

So I’d want to ask how well it fits the data, what alternatives fit, and especially whether it predicts performance on tasks longer than the ones you used to fit it. I’d be much more comfortable using it as a rough empirical summary than extrapolating it very far.

r001.rationale: It says a constant hazard rate means the probability of completing the whole task falls exponentially with task length, which conveys exponential decay in AI success as human task duration increases.
